profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab after a reproduction attempt of a paper on variance in neural network training reports a contradiction: the lab's repeated ResNet-50 and ViT-B fine-tuning runs show much larger spread than expected, and the estimated 'distribution-level' accuracy also appears unstable. The context is that the team is preparing an internal note before deciding whether the issue is a bug in evaluation, a mismatch in protocol, or a genuine failure of the claimed phenomenon under fine-tuning and mild shift. The agenda is to diagnose why the current reruns do not match the paper's core claim, identify the most plausible root cause, and agree on a minimal fix to rerun by the end of the week. The expected outcome is an agreed troubleshooting plan for one revised experiment setup and one validation check.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: generalization, uncertainty estimation, and empirical analysis of deep learning experiments
members.background: Maya leads the lab's reliability-focused empirical studies and has previously worked on calibration and distribution-shift benchmarks; she designed the current reproduction plan and wrote the analysis notebook for run-to-run variance.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the broader interpretation that the paper's conclusions should extend at least qualitatively to fine-tuning settings, and she is worried that a simple implementation mistake in her pipeline would undermine confidence in her recent internal results.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing the 'test distribution,' a Monte Carlo estimate formed by evaluating each trained checkpoint on multiple stochastic augmentation draws is an acceptable proxy for the underlying distribution.
The main troubleshooting target is the mismatch in the variance decomposition analysis rather than any single model run, because the claim should be robust to ordinary training noise.
A 'rerun with the standard setup' still includes the lab's default evaluation-time crop/resize and mixed-precision inference settings unless someone explicitly says to disable them.
If repeated runs are compared under the same nominal hyperparameters, differences induced by checkpoint selection details are second-order and not the likely root cause.

members.name: Ethan Park
members.expertise: training infrastructure, evaluation pipelines, and reproducible experiment execution at scale
members.background: Ethan maintains the lab's ImageNet and CIFAR evaluation stack, recently migrated several jobs to a new launcher, and implemented the automated sweep that produced the anomalous variance numbers.
members.private_state: He wants to rule out infrastructure issues quickly and keep the fix small, because cluster time is tight and he is concerned the anomaly may come from an unnoticed protocol mismatch introduced during the launcher migration.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'test distribution,' they mean the conceptual population approximated by the fixed official test split, not a stochastic augmentation-induced distribution created at evaluation time.
The practical troubleshooting target is to reproduce the paper's exact test-set protocol before interpreting any theoretical claim, because infrastructure drift is the dominant failure mode.
A 'standard setup' means deterministic center-crop evaluation in full precision on the official validation/test split, since that is the canonical baseline for reproducibility.
Checkpoint selection matters materially: using the last epoch versus best validation epoch can easily change apparent run-to-run spread enough to explain the issue.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the runs are stable on the 'test distribution.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an estimate of accuracy over a broader input distribution induced by repeated stochastic test-time augmentation around each labeled example, used as a practical stand-in for the underlying distribution.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the population represented by the official fixed test/validation set, with no extra stochasticity added at evaluation beyond the canonical deterministic preprocessing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research conversation, 'test distribution' is a familiar phrase and both interpretations sound technically respectable; because both are discussing variance beyond a finite test set, each hears the other's wording as confirming their own meaning.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to rerun under the 'standard setup' to remove confounds.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes the lab's current default stack: mixed-precision inference, resize-then-random-crop for evaluation on augmented views, and the same launcher defaults used in recent projects.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes the paper-faithful baseline stack: deterministic center crop, full-precision evaluation, and the original single-view official split protocol.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe the phrase refers to an already-settled baseline everyone in the lab knows, so neither expects that 'standard' itself needs unpacking during a troubleshooting meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss finding a 'minimal fix' before the end of the week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the fix is successful if the revised analysis restores low variance in the estimated distribution-level metric and preserves the paper's qualitative story, even if test-set spread remains noisy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the fix is successful if repeated runs under an exact paper-like protocol produce a narrow enough spread on the fixed evaluation split to match the reported tables, regardless of any auxiliary distribution estimate.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same troubleshooting language about 'fixing the discrepancy,' but in research debugging it is common to collapse different validation standards into a single phrase, especially when both standards seem aligned with the same paper.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to rerun evaluation with the 'selected checkpoint' from each training run.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the final training checkpoint at epoch 90, because her variance notebook indexes runs by terminal state and treats checkpoint choice as part of the training trajectory.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the best-validation checkpoint automatically saved by the launcher, because the sweep dashboard labels that artifact as the selected checkpoint for each run.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both refer to a single checkpoint per run and assume the other is looking at the obvious artifact; the term 'selected checkpoint' sounds unambiguous because each workflow has only one default notion of selection.

turns.inner_thought: The main problem isn't one odd run; it's that the variance decomposition in my notebook is not lining up with the paper's story, and that makes our internal note shaky. I'm especially concerned because the test distribution estimate, where I average over multiple stochastic augmentation draws per checkpoint, is still moving more than it should across seeds. If that's real, it weakens the broader qualitative extension to fine-tuning that I think should hold. I also really hope this isn't a simple bug in my pipeline.
turns.utterance: Thanks for jumping on this. Right now the reproduction is still showing a much bigger run-to-run spread than the paper would suggest, and what's blocking the note for me is that performance on the test distribution also looks surprisingly unstable. Until we understand that, it's hard to say whether we're seeing a real contradiction or just something off in the setup.

turns.inner_thought: This still smells like infrastructure drift from the launcher migration. Before anyone reads theory into the numbers, we need to get back to the exact paper-faithful protocol on the fixed official split with deterministic evaluation. 'Standard setup' should mean the canonical baseline, not whatever defaults have crept into recent jobs. If I can keep this to a small protocol correction, we save cluster time.
turns.utterance: My first guess is still a protocol mismatch from the launcher migration. I think we should rerun the analysis under the standard setup before we interpret the paper's claim too much. If something drifted in the eval path, that could easily inflate the spread without saying anything interesting about the result itself.

turns.inner_thought: I'm fine with a rerun under the standard setup, meaning the lab defaults we've been using lately. But the symptom I care about is that even after averaging over augmented views, the distribution-level estimate is wandering too much across seeds. That shouldn't happen if this is just ordinary finite-sample noise. I need to steer us toward the analysis layer without sounding defensive.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I'm on board with using the standard setup to strip away confounds. What still bothers me is that even after averaging things out, the estimate on the test distribution is moving a lot across seeds. So to me the mismatch doesn't look like just a single noisy pass.

turns.inner_thought: If evaluation is truly deterministic on the official split, then most of what remains should be training variance plus any checkpoint-selection effect. And checkpoint choice can absolutely matter; last epoch versus best validation can change the spread a lot. I need to check whether Maya's notebook is actually using the launcher's selected artifact.
turns.utterance: That makes sense, but if the evaluation pass is deterministic then most of the remaining spread should really be coming from training. Are we definitely comparing the selected checkpoint for each run, rather than mixing artifacts in some way?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the notebook is keyed to the terminal checkpoint for each run; that's the selected checkpoint in my workflow. I don't think checkpoint details are the main culprit anyway, especially when the variance decomposition still looks off after grouping by nominal hyperparameters. The broader pattern should be robust to ordinary training noise and minor selection differences.
turns.utterance: Yes, the selected checkpoint is what feeds the notebook. And even when I group the fine-tuned runs by the same nominal hyperparameters, the variance decomposition still looks wrong, which is why I don't think this is just one bad run slipping through.

turns.inner_thought: Let's keep this small and decisive: ten seeds, canonical evaluation, fixed validation split, and see whether the spread matches the tables. That's the minimal fix I can justify with current cluster pressure. If the numbers collapse there, we can stop blaming the training story and focus on protocol drift.
turns.utterance: Given the time pressure, I'd suggest a minimal fix first: rerun ten seeds under the standard setup and check whether the spread on the validation split collapses to something close to the paper's tables. If that happens, we'll have a much cleaner read on whether this is mostly a reproducibility issue.

turns.inner_thought: A minimal fix is reasonable, but success for me is whether the qualitative claim survives at the level of the distribution estimate, not just whether a fixed-split table looks nicer. Finite test-set noise alone shouldn't explain the whole discrepancy if the phenomenon is real, especially in fine-tuning. I need him aligned enough to preserve that check.
turns.utterance: I agree a minimal fix makes sense. I mainly want to make sure we still look at whether the qualitative claim survives on the test distribution, because finite test-set noise by itself shouldn't be driving the whole discrepancy if the underlying story is intact.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, she can keep her broader metric, but only after we verify the canonical path. If the launcher changed eval mode or the run is pointing at a different saved artifact, then the instability is an artifact, not evidence about the claim. I need to make checkpoint choice and eval protocol the first gate without opening a big philosophical detour.
turns.utterance: That's fine with me, as long as we first verify the canonical eval path. If the selected checkpoint or the eval mode drifted during the migration, then the instability could just be an artifact of the stack rather than anything deeper.

turns.inner_thought: To separate an analysis bug from a training issue quickly, we should start by re-evaluating the checkpoints we already have. In my mind that's the final epoch artifacts already indexed in the notebook. If those stabilize under the same broad evaluation view, I can stop worrying that the underlying result fails under fine-tuning and maybe trace this back to the variance code.
turns.utterance: Then maybe the fastest move is to keep everything else fixed and just re-evaluate the selected checkpoint artifacts we already have. That should let us separate analysis issues from retraining issues without waiting on a full new sweep.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I can re-run evaluation on the launcher-tagged best checkpoints and regenerate metrics with the canonical deterministic path. That gives us a clean baseline against the current numbers and avoids spending compute before we know whether the migration changed something obvious.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I can do that. I'll regenerate the metrics under the standard setup as well so we have a clean baseline against the current numbers, and then we can see whether the discrepancy survives that comparison.

turns.inner_thought: If the revised evaluation restores stability in the distribution-level estimate, I'll treat this as mostly an evaluation-layer problem and not as evidence against the paper's variance argument carrying over qualitatively to fine-tuning. That would also make me feel a lot better about the recent internal results and the notebook.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. If the revised pass restores stability on the test distribution, I'll be pretty comfortable treating this as mostly an evaluation-layer bug rather than evidence against the variance argument itself.

turns.inner_thought: Plan is clear enough: this afternoon I'll rerun the existing selected checkpoints using the canonical baseline, then report whether variance on the fixed official split is back in line by Friday. If yes, that's the minimal fix. If no, then we can talk about retraining or deeper analysis. Hopefully this stays small.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll rerun the selected checkpoints this afternoon and report back by Friday on whether the variance under the standard setup now matches what we'd expect. If it does, we can treat that as the minimal fix and decide whether any follow-up is still needed for the note.
